title: 1 Samuel 5:1–5
context: The Philistines bring the captured ark to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon in his temple, but on two successive mornings Dagon is found fallen on his face before the ark, the second time with head and hands broken off on the threshold. The narrator notes a later custom of not stepping on Dagon’s threshold. Both traditions read this as shared ground: the LORD is not defeated by Israel’s loss, and he humbles the idols of the nations.

verses.text: Now the Philistines had taken God’s ark, and they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines bring God’s ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod. Arminian readers note that the narrative now follows the ark rather than Israel.

The ark’s capture is not the end of the story; God will act on his own behalf.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the scene shift from Israel’s defeat to God’s vindication of his name.

The ark goes into enemy territory, where the LORD will show that he has not been defeated.

verses.text: The Philistines took God’s ark, and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it by Dagon.
verses.arminianNotes:
They set the ark in the house of Dagon beside Dagon. Arminian readers note that placing it there suggests a trophy displayed before the Philistines’ god.

Dagon’s exact identity and character are debated, so the notes do not define him further.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a direct confrontation between the LORD and an idol in the idol’s own temple.

The Philistines treat the ark as a captured deity, but the following verses overturn that assumption.

verses.text: When the people of Ashdod arose early on the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the LORD’s ark. They took Dagon and set him in his place again.
verses.arminianNotes:
The next morning Dagon has fallen on his face to the ground before the LORD’s ark, and they set him in his place again. Arminian readers note the posture, which looks like an act of homage or defeat.

The people must lift their god back up.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the idol prostrate before the true God, recalling God’s judgment on the gods of Egypt (Exod 12:12).

That Dagon must be set up by human hands shows his helplessness (cf. Isa 46:1–2).

verses.text: When they arose early on the following morning, behold, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the LORD’s ark; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off on the threshold. Only Dagon’s torso was intact.
verses.arminianNotes:
The next morning Dagon has fallen again, with his head and both palms cut off on the threshold; only his torso remains. Arminian readers note the escalation from the first morning.

The broken image leaves no doubt about which God is supreme.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the complete humiliation of the idol (cf. Ps 115:4–8).

The severed head and hands picture an idol with neither mind nor power to act. This is shared ground about God’s holiness.

verses.text: Therefore neither the priests of Dagon nor any who come into Dagon’s house step on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore Dagon’s priests and worshipers do not step on his threshold in Ashdod “to this day.” Arminian readers note that the narrator explains a custom known at the time of writing.

Some readers connect Zephaniah 1:9 with such threshold customs, as a reading.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a lasting memorial of Dagon’s defeat.

The custom ironically commemorates the very event that showed Dagon’s powerlessness before the LORD.
